sections.title: 🧩 Base Shifting Logic
sections.content: Base shifting occurs when the reference point (the 100% base) changes during a calculation. The golden rule is the fractional shift: If a value increases by 1/n, to return to the original value, it must decrease by 1/(n+1). Conversely, if it decreases by 1/n, it must increase by 1/(n-1). Example: If the price of petrol increases by 25% (1/4), consumption must decrease by 20% (1/5) to keep the expenditure constant. In monetary terms, if Aman's salary is ₹60,000, which is 20% (1/5) more than Bina's, then Bina's salary is strictly 16.66% (1/6) less than Aman's. Bina's salary = ₹60,000 - (1/6 × 60,000) = ₹50,000.

sections.title: ➕➖ Net Effect of +x% and -x%
sections.content: A common trap is assuming that an increase of x% followed by a decrease of x% brings you back to the original value. The reality is a strict mathematical net loss, calculated universally as (x²/100)%. This happens because the subsequent decrease acts on a larger, newly inflated base. Example: An investor puts ₹5,00,000 into a mutual fund. In year one, it surges by 20%. In year two, a market correction causes a 20% drop. The net loss is (20²/100)% = 4%. The absolute loss is 4% of ₹5,00,000 = ₹20,000. Final portfolio value = ₹4,80,000.

sections.title: 🔍 Hidden Base Problems
sections.content: Ultra-hard percentage problems often disguise the true base by manipulating a mixture where only one component changes. The master trick is to identify the 'Constant Component' and equate its absolute mass before and after the change. Example: 80 kg of fresh mushrooms contain 90% water (meaning 10% solid pulp). After drying, they contain 20% water (meaning 80% solid pulp). The solid pulp remains mathematically identical. Solid Pulp = 10% of 80 kg = 8 kg. In the dry state, this 8 kg represents 80% of the new total weight. Therefore, 80% of Dry Weight = 8 kg. Dry Weight = 10 kg. If the dry mushrooms sell for ₹1,200/kg, the total revenue is ₹12,000.

sections.title: 💹 Multi-Step Percent Changes
sections.content: For successive percentage changes, discard the traditional additive formulas and embrace Multiplicative Fraction Chaining. Convert every percentage change into a scaling multiplier. Example: A luxury car originally priced at ₹25,00,000 depreciates by 14.28% (1/7) in year one, appreciates by 12.5% (1/8) due to a vintage mod in year two, and depreciates by 10% (1/10) in year three. Multipliers: (1 - 1/7) = 6/7; (1 + 1/8) = 9/8; (1 - 1/10) = 9/10. Final Value = ₹25,00,000 × (6/7) × (9/8) × (9/10) = ₹25,00,000 × (486/560) ≈ ₹21,69,642. This chain perfectly bypasses irrational decimal loops.

sections.title: 📐 Concept Framework
sections.content: To conquer Level 3 percentage questions, apply this 4-pillar framework: 1. Anchor Identification: Pinpoint the exact entity representing 100%. 2. Fraction Conversion: Instantly convert complex percentages (e.g., 16.66%, 8.33%, 37.5%) into pure fractions (1/6, 1/12, 3/8) to neutralize decimals. 3. Zero-Sum Mapping: In expenditure or product equations (A × B = Constant), force the multiplier of A to exactly invert the multiplier of B. 4. Component Isolation: In Venn diagrams or mixture problems, track the components that do not overlap or do not evaporate.

sections.title: ⚡ Advanced Summary
sections.content: Percentages are not absolute numbers; they are elastic relations tethered to shifting bases. Mastering Ultra-Hard percentages requires abandoning the 'assume 100' crutch when dealing with nasty fractions. Instead, assume the LCM of the fractional denominators as your base. Recognize that successive +x% and -y% changes commute (order doesn't matter). Always isolate the invariant absolute value—whether it's the fixed pulp in a drying fruit, the constant valid votes in an election, or the unchanging savings in a budget shift—and build your percentage equations around that absolute rock.

tricks.title: ➕➖ Net Effect Shortcut
tricks.explanation: When a value is successively increased by x% and then decreased by exactly x% (or vice versa), the result is NEVER the original number. There is always a strict net loss, and the net loss percentage is universally equal to (x²/100)%.
tricks.example: A jewelry store marks up a gold necklace worth ₹80,000 by 25% and then offers a 25% festive discount. Net loss = (25²/100)% = 6.25%. Final Selling Price = ₹80,000 - 6.25% = ₹75,000.

tricks.title: 🔗 Multi-Layer Fractional Chaining
tricks.explanation: For 3 or more successive percentage changes, abandon the cumbersome a+b+(ab/100) formula. Convert all percentages to unitary fraction multipliers (1 ± x/100) and multiply them sequentially. This perfectly neutralizes messy repeating decimals.

tricks.title: 🔄 Inverse Base Transformation
tricks.explanation: If variable A is strictly a/b more than base B, then base B is exactly a/(a+b) less than A. Conversely, if A is a/b less than B, then B is exactly a/(b-a) more than A. This bypasses the need to set variables to 100x.
tricks.example: Neha earns 20% (1/5) less than Rohan. Using the rule, Rohan earns 1/(5-1) = 1/4 = 25% more than Neha. If Neha earns ₹60,000, Rohan earns ₹60,000 + 25% = ₹75,000.

tricks.title: ⚖️ Constant Product & Expenditure Rule
tricks.explanation: When Price × Consumption = Expenditure (and Expenditure must remain constant): If price increases by a fraction a/b, consumption must be reduced by the fraction a/(a+b).
tricks.example: The price of petrol surges by 16.66% (1/6). To keep the monthly fuel budget strictly pegged at ₹4,200, driving distance (consumption) must drop by 1/(6+1) = 1/7, which is 14.28%.

tricks.title: 🪤 Trap Identification: Profit on SP
tricks.explanation: Examiners trap high-level candidates by stating profit as a percentage of the Selling Price (SP) rather than Cost Price (CP). A false profit of 1/n on SP translates to a true mathematical profit of 1/(n-1) on CP.
tricks.example: A merchant claims a 20% (1/5) profit calculated on his SP. True profit on CP = 1/(5-1) = 1/4 = 25%. If his SP is ₹15,000, his CP is ₹12,000 (yielding a ₹3,000 profit), not ₹12,500.

tricks.title: ⚗️ The Constant Component Mixture Equation
tricks.explanation: In complex evaporation, drying, or dilution problems, completely ignore the substance that is changing. Equate the absolute mass or volume of the constant (unchanging) component: Initial Volume × %Constant₁ = Final Volume × %Constant₂.
tricks.example: 60 kg of fresh watermelon contains 90% water (10% pulp). After lying in the sun, it dries to 60% water (40% pulp). Constant Pulp Equation: 60 kg × 10% = Dry Weight × 40%. Dry Weight = 15 kg worth ₹750.

tricks.title: 🎯 Alligation for Blended Percentages
tricks.explanation: When mixing two separate groups with distinct percentage attributes to achieve a combined mean percentage, the cross-difference of their percentages instantly yields the ratio of their base quantities.
tricks.example: A ₹2,00,000 fund is split between Equity (+18% return) and Debt (+6% return). The overall portfolio yield is +10%. Ratio of Equity:Debt = |6 - 10| : |18 - 10| = 4 : 8 = 1:2. Equity allocation = 1/3 of ₹2,00,000 = ₹66,666.67.

tricks.title: 🕵️ Tax Rate vs Net Income Parity
tricks.explanation: When a flat tax rate increases and gross salary is constant, the absolute increase in the tax deducted perfectly equals the absolute decrease in net take-home pay. Change in Tax = Drop in Net Income.
tricks.example: The income tax rate shifts from 15% to 18%, causing Vivek's net take-home pay to drop by exactly ₹3,600. This ₹3,600 is the 3% difference in gross income. Gross Income = ₹3,600 / 0.03 = ₹1,20,000.

tricks.title: ⚖️ Dishonest Dealer Weight Multiplier
tricks.explanation: For dishonest dealers, treat the faulty weight purely as a fractional multiplier on the cost price base. Faulty Multiplier = (True Weight / Claimed Weight). Multiply this sequentially with standard markup and discount multipliers.
tricks.example: A grocer marks up by 20% (6/5), gives a 10% discount (9/10), and uses an 800g weight instead of 1kg (1000/800 = 5/4). Net multiplier = (6/5) × (9/10) × (5/4) = 270/200 = 1.35. He makes a 35% net profit on a ₹5,000 investment.

tricks.title: 📉 The 'Remaining' Residual Cascade Trap
tricks.explanation: When spending percentages of 'the remaining' amount successively, DO NOT subtract the percentages from 100 linearly. The final residual amount strictly equals Initial × (1 - P₁/100) × (1 - P₂/100).
tricks.example: Pooja spends 20% of her ₹80,000 salary on EMI, then 30% of the *remaining* on lifestyle. Residual = ₹80,000 × (4/5) × (7/10) = ₹44,800. (Trap: It is NOT 50% remaining, which would be ₹40,000).

tricks.title: 🗳️ Voting Base Identification Trap
tricks.explanation: In election questions, explicitly check if the winner's percentage is based on the 'Total Electoral List' or 'Valid Votes Cast'. If based on the Total List, invalid votes act as a direct absolute numeric penalty strictly against the loser's tally.
tricks.example: Winner gets 48% of the *Total* List. 10% didn't vote. Invalid votes = 1,200. Loser gets (90% - 48%) - 1,200 = 42% - 1,200. The winning margin is 48% - (42% - 1,200) = 6% + 1,200. If margin is 4,800, then 6% = 3,600, so Total List = 60,000 voters.

tricks.title: 🔁 Percentage Reciprocal Cancellation
tricks.explanation: Identify complementary repeating decimal percentages that act as exact mathematical reciprocals. They perfectly neutralize each other during successive multiplier calculations, bypassing arithmetic entirely.
tricks.example: A vintage artifact worth ₹1,56,000 appreciates by 14.28% (multiplier 8/7) in year one, then depreciates by exactly 12.5% (multiplier 7/8) in year two. Final value = ₹1,56,000 × (8/7) × (7/8) = ₹1,56,000. Net change is mathematically zero.
